js_004: Who wrote The Dwarf Launches a Little Ball?
js_009: The Dwarf Launches a Little Ball is a linked-story cycle Cho Se-hui completed in 1978. It’s often shortened to just The Dwarf.
js_011: Which best describes this work’s form?
js_012: A cycle of twelve linked stories
js_013: An anthology co-written by several authors
js_016: The Dwarf is a cycle of twelve linked stories sharing characters and setting. From “The Blade” to “Epilogue,” they weave into one.
js_018: What physical trait does the family’s father have?
js_023: The father has dwarfism — he’s a dwarf. People simply called him “the dwarf” and nothing else.
js_025: What are the names of the dwarf’s three children?
js_030: The three siblings are eldest Yeong-su, second Yeong-ho, and youngest daughter Yeong-hui. Their viewpoints drive the story.
js_032: What’s the name of the neighborhood facing demolition, where the family lives?
js_034: Machine Town, in the factory city of Eungang
js_037: The family lives in Eden District, Happy Town. A slum with neither Eden nor happiness — the name itself is bitter irony.
js_039: What notice arrives and sets the story in motion?
js_040: A demolition notice ordering the house torn down
js_042: A draft notice for military service
js_043: A court summons to repay a debt
js_044: The story opens with a demolition notice. This single sheet of paper, ordering them out for redevelopment, pushes the family to the edge.
js_046: What single document does the family receive because of the redevelopment?
js_048: A deed to a large plot of land
js_051: The family gets move-in rights to an apartment — a voucher. But with no money for the extra payment, they sell it cheap to a speculator.
js_053: Where does the dwarf father take his own life?
js_055: On a large bridge over the river
js_056: On the rooftop of an old apartment block
js_057: At the end of a harbor breakwater
js_058: The father climbs the brick factory smokestack, launches a little ball toward the moon, and throws himself from it. The novel’s most painful scene.
js_060: As the title says, what does the father launch toward the moon?
js_065: From atop the smokestack, the father launches a little steel ball toward the moon — a symbol of a dream for an unreachable, ideal world.
js_067: When was this story cycle published as a single collected volume?
js_072: The Dwarf was collected into one volume by Munhakgwajisung-sa in 1978. It won the Dong-in Literary Award in 1979.

js_082: Cho Se-hui (1942–2022) debuted in 1965 and left a lasting mark on Korean literature with The Dwarf, his portrait of 1970s industrialization’s dark side.
js_083: The Dwarf is a cycle of twelve linked stories, from “Möbius Strip” to “Epilogue,” sharing characters and setting. You can read any one alone, or all in order.
js_084: The father has dwarfism. He’s hardworking, but the world called him only “the dwarf,” never his name — his body a symbol of the marginalized and powerless.
js_085: The three siblings — Yeong-su, Yeong-ho, Yeong-hui — each fight poverty in their own way. Their viewpoints take turns carrying the story.
js_086: Eden District, Happy Town is a slum on the brink of demolition, with neither Eden nor happiness in sight. The gap between the glossy name and grim reality captures the novel’s irony.
js_087: The demolition notice orders the family to vacate. This single sheet of paper is what pushes the family to the very edge of survival.
js_088: The family receives apartment move-in rights — a voucher — but has no money for the extra payment. They end up selling it cheap to a speculator and lose their home.
js_089: The dwarf father climbs the brick factory smokestack, launches a little ball toward the moon, then throws himself from it — his final gesture toward an ideal world with no place for him.
js_090: The little steel ball launched from the smokestack symbolizes a dream of the moon — a world without discrimination. Its unreachability makes it all the more heartbreaking.
js_091: The Dwarf was published as a single volume by Munhakgwajisung-sa in 1978. It has remained a steady bestseller ever since.
js_105: The dwarf father Kim Bul-i, his wife, and their three children — Yeong-su, Yeong-ho, Yeong-hui. The face of the urban poor in the industrial era: hardworking, yet unable to escape poverty.
js_107: Along with the demolition notice comes an apartment move-in voucher. Unable to pay the extra fee, the family sells it cheap to a speculator and loses their home — redevelopment pushing the poor out.
js_108: The little ball and the moon
js_109: The little steel ball the father launches toward the moon from the smokestack. A dream of an ideal world free of oppression — but like the ball, it never reaches the moon, and is ultimately crushed.
js_111: A shape where inside and outside connect, erasing the line between victimizer and victim. The math teacher’s story in the opening chapter becomes the key to the whole work.
js_113: Eungang, the industrial city where Yeong-su and Yeong-ho go to work. Low wages, long hours, and the crushing of labor organizing — another wall the family runs into.
js_115: The clash between the powerless dwarf and the “giant” who represents the haves. The Eungang conglomerate wears the giant’s face, condensing the conflict between capital and labor.
js_117: The youngest daughter follows the real-estate broker and cracks his safe to reclaim the stolen voucher. But even getting it back can’t undo her father’s death.
js_119: The author’s style — short, dry sentences that render brutal reality plainly, layered with fairy-tale-like fantasy. The form itself is what makes the impact land.
js_122: A math teacher tells his students the story of the Möbius strip.
js_123: It hints at a world where inside and outside merge, erasing the line between victimizer and victim.
js_124: It becomes the symbolic gateway opening all twelve stories to come.
js_125: It raises, in advance, the question of who the real oppressor is.
js_127: Happy Town — “The Blade,” “Space Travel,” “The Dwarf Launches a Little Ball”
js_128: A demolition notice arrives in Happy Town, where the dwarf’s family lives.
js_129: They receive apartment move-in rights but sell them cheap for lack of funds.
js_130: Yeong-hui leaves home, following the broker to reclaim the voucher.
js_131: The father launches a little ball toward the moon from the smokestack, and dies.
js_133: A family scattered — “On the Overpass,” “Orbital Rotation”
js_134: Having lost their father, the family begins to scatter.
js_135: Each struggles to survive at the bottom rung of the city.
js_136: Like an orbit, poverty keeps circling back no matter how hard they try to escape.
js_137: Even small hopes keep getting crushed by the city’s cold indifference.
js_139: The factories of Eungang — “Machine City,” “The Cost of Living for an Eungang Working Family,” “God Is at Fault Too”
js_140: Yeong-su and Yeong-ho become factory workers in the industrial city of Eungang.
js_141: Low wages, long hours, and a razor-thin cost of living are laid bare.
js_142: Yeong-su fights for workers’ rights but hits a wall.
js_143: God Is at Fault Too — a cry against the absurdity of the system erupts.
js_145: Caught in the net — “Klein’s Bottle,” “The Stickleback That Swims Into My Net”
js_146: A world tangled like a Klein bottle, inside and outside indistinguishable, is drawn once more.
js_147: The final chapter is told from the viewpoint of Gyeong-hun, the chairman’s son.
js_148: Yeong-su kills the chairman’s brother by mistake and is sentenced to death.
js_149: The cold gaze of the haves makes the tragedy even more chilling.
js_152: The unreached dream of the moon lingers like an afterimage.
js_153: It has become a classic of Korean literature, bearing witness to the dark side of 1970s industrialization.
js_154: Printed in the hundreds since publication, it remains a steady bestseller today.
js_155: Who’s responsible when hard work still isn’t enough to escape poverty? The question still stands.
js_156: The voucher sold for a pittance
js_157: The family gets apartment move-in rights, but with no money for the extra payment, they sell the voucher cheap to a speculator buying them up. Redevelopment, meant to house them, ends up taking their home instead.
js_158: It’s worth considering how a system that looks like welfare can become a device that pushes out the vulnerable — that’s the paradox here.
js_159: The dwarf father climbs the brick factory smokestack, launches a little ball toward the moon, and throws himself from it. His final gesture toward an ideal world that had no place for him.
js_160: Why does a death that looks like pure defeat stay with readers for so long? It’s worth asking what the dream really means.
js_162: Broken by the failure of the labor movement, Yeong-su goes after the Eungang chairman but kills his lookalike brother instead, and is sentenced to death. A structural contradiction that explodes as one man’s rage.
js_163: When the system blocks every path, where should individual resistance turn? It leaves a heavy question behind.
js_164: If hard work still can’t lift you out of poverty, whose fault is that?
js_165: Think of all the odd jobs the dwarf father took on. It’s a prompt to consider problems that individual effort alone can’t solve.
js_166: Is the little ball the dwarf launches an empty escape, or is it a form of resistance?
js_167: Consider what it means to keep dreaming even while knowing the moon can never be reached.
js_168: When the Möbius strip blurs the line between victimizer and victim, where do we stand?
js_169: Read it as a question of whether you, too, might be someone else’s giant.
